titleEn: Acute Pulmonary Edema at 0300 - Sitting Upright, CPAP

patient.name: George Whitfield
patient.affectEn: awake, alert and anxious; sitting bolt upright on the edge of the bed, leaning forward with his hands on his knees and his feet on the floor, using his shoulders and neck to breathe; pale and glistening with sweat; says it feels like he is drowning. He will not lie back - if he is laid back or flat he panics and sits bolt upright again.
patient.speechEn: answers in 3-4 word phrases between breaths (can't... catch... my breath); cooperative and follows simple commands. His wife fills in most of the history while he can only manage short phrases.

scene.settingEn: Second-floor bedroom of a townhouse in Coquitlam at 0300 hrs, reached by a narrow staircase. The lights are on and the room is at normal temperature. His wife stands in the doorway holding a bag of his medications. One patient. Fire is not attending; the hospital is 12 minutes away.
hazardsEn: none identified - the narrow staircase to the second floor is the only way out

bystanders.knowsEn: Stands in the doorway holding a bag of his medications; she will hold doors, fetch things and carry the medication bag if asked, and fills in the history while he can only manage short phrases. He woke at about 0245, about 25 minutes before you arrived, gasping and saying he was drowning; he had to sit up and still could not get his breath. Cough with a little pink-tinged frothy sputum. More breathless on stairs for two weeks, three pillows for the last week, ankles swollen for several days, tired and weak for a week. He ran out of his furosemide 3 days ago. He has not used his nitroglycerin spray tonight. No fever, no nausea or vomiting, no fall or injury.

scene.partnerEn: one partner at your licence level; acts only on your delegation
equipmentEn: oxygen kit with non-rebreather mask and nasal cannula
adult BVM with oxygen tubing and reservoir
his own nitroglycerin spray (in the medication bag)
PCP only: CPAP device with masks and valves, PEEP valve for the BVM, ipratropium, IV start kit

dispatchEn: 0300 hrs. Code 3 to a townhouse in Coquitlam. 74-year-old male with severe shortness of breath; his wife says he woke up unable to breathe. Fire is not attending. Hospital is 12 minutes away.
dispatchUpdateEn: Dispatch update en route: his wife says he is sitting on the edge of the bed leaning forward and cannot lie down. The bedroom is on the second floor, up a narrow staircase. She will leave the front door unlocked and wait for you at the top of the stairs.
arrivalEn: The front door is unlocked. His wife meets you at the top of the narrow staircase and leads you into the second-floor bedroom, where she stands in the doorway holding a bag of his medications. The lights are on and the room is at normal temperature. No hazards. One patient. Your partner is right behind you with the kits.
firstLookEn: A 74-year-old man sitting bolt upright on the edge of the bed, leaning forward with his hands on his knees and his feet on the floor, using his shoulders and neck to breathe. His skin is pale and glistening with sweat. He is too breathless to say more than a few words at a time.

primary.locEn: Awake and alert (AVPU = A), anxious. He answers in 3-4 word phrases and says it feels like he is drowning. He follows simple commands. If the candidate lays him back or flat he panics, becomes more breathless and sits bolt upright again.
primary.airwayEn: Patent. Wet, gurgly voice. A little pink-tinged frothy sputum when he coughs. No stridor. Keep suction at hand.
primary.breathingEn: Respirations 32, laboured with accessory muscle use; he speaks only 3-4 words at a time. Bilateral crackles to the mid-fields with a few expiratory wheezes; air entry equal; chest rise symmetrical.
primary.circulationEn: Radial pulse 112, strong and regular. No external bleeding.
primary.rbsEn: Modified rapid body survey for a medical patient: no trauma; both ankles are swollen with pitting edema. Skin pale, cool and sweaty (skin is given automatically during the RBS). C-spine is not indicated.

opqrst.oEn: It woke me up... about quarter to three. Gasping. Felt like... I was drowning. It came on suddenly.
opqrst.pEn: Worse lying flat... and when I move. Only a little better... sitting up.
opqrst.qEn: Like I'm drowning... I can't get a breath in.
opqrst.rEn: No chest pain. No chest pressure. No pain anywhere.
opqrst.sEn: The worst breathless... I've ever been.
opqrst.tEn: (Wife:) It started about 25 minutes before you got here - he woke at about quarter to three.

history.painScoreEn: None - no chest pain, no chest pressure and no pain anywhere.

sample.sEn: Cough... pink frothy spit. Heart's racing... sweating. (Wife:) He's been more breathless on stairs for two weeks, needing three pillows for the last week, and his ankles have been swollen for several days.
sample.mEn: (Wife:) Furosemide 40 milligrams a day - he ran out 3 days ago. Ramipril 5 milligrams a day, metoprolol 50 milligrams twice a day, atorvastatin 20 milligrams a day, and his nitroglycerin spray if he needs it - he hasn't used it tonight.
sample.pEn: Heart failure... a heart attack with a stent... 6 years ago. High blood pressure. High cholesterol.
sample.lEn: Dinner at 6 o'clock... just water by the bed since.
sample.eEn: (Wife:) He woke up gasping at about quarter to three, saying he was drowning, and had to sit up. No fever, no nausea or vomiting, and no fall or injury.

fe.generalEn: Tired... and weak... for a week.
fe.respiratoryEn: Breathless on stairs... two weeks. Three pillows... last week. Cough with frothy spit. Breathing easier... on the mask.
fe.cardiovascularEn: Heart racing. Ankles swollen... several days. No chest pain.
fe.giGuEn: Bloated... poor appetite. Passing less urine... since the furosemide ran out. No nausea. No vomiting.
fe.integumentaryEn: Sweaty. Skin cool. Ankles tight... and swollen.

findings.headNeckEn: Jugular veins distended while sitting upright, trachea midline, no trauma.
findings.chestLungsEn: Fine crackles from the bases to the mid-fields on 6-site auscultation, a few expiratory wheezes, air entry equal, chest rise symmetrical, no tenderness.
findings.backEn: Fine crackles posteriorly, no trauma or tenderness.
findings.lowerExtremitiesEn: Pitting edema to mid-shin on both sides, pulses present, CSM intact.
findings.upperExtremitiesEn: No edema, radial pulses strong, CSM intact.

He has become drowsy, and his breathing has become slow and shallow.

expected.actionEn: Acknowledge; plan oxygen, upright positioning, CPAP (PCP) or BVM, a stair chair / carry device and early transport
triggers: I'm planning for a breathing call

expected.actionEn: Recognize from dispatch a likely unstable respiratory-distress call: severe shortness of breath, unable to lie down
Fire is not attending: consider additional resources (e.g. First Responders) to help carry him down the stairs (p.10)
triggers: need help to carry him down

expected.actionEn: Anticipate a coughing patient: PPE incl eye protection
triggers: PPE ready before we go in

expected.actionEn: Verbalize hazards (none; narrow stairs), environment, nature of illness (severe shortness of breath, possible cardiac cause), number of patients (1)
triggers: nature of illness is shortness of breath

expected.actionEn: Don gloves and eye protection (coughing patient)
triggers: putting on gloves and eye protection

expected.actionEn: First look: sitting forward in a tripod position, shoulder and neck muscles working, a few words at a time, pale and sweaty
Plan egress: narrow staircase means a seated carry (stair chair / carry device); bring the equipment to the patient and keep his exertion to a minimum (p.33)
Assess LOC / AVPU: Alert; check that he follows commands (needed for the CPAP decision)
Verbalize c-spine not indicated (medical, no trauma)
Assess airway: patent but wet voice and frothy sputum, no stridor; have suction ready
Assess breathing: rate, effort, accessory muscle use, speech; auscultate both sides (crackles, wheezes, equal air entry)
triggers: how many words can he say

expected.actionEn: Assess circulation: radial pulse rate, strength and regularity
Perform the rapid body survey: no trauma; find the swollen ankles (pitting edema)
Note skin: pale, cool, sweaty
High-flow oxygen 15 L NRB now, titrate to SpO2 94% or higher; if still below 94% add a nasal cannula under the mask at 15 L/min (p.33, p.50)
triggers: add a nasal cannula under the mask

expected.actionEn: Keep him sitting upright with his legs hung down - do not lay him back; keep him at rest and warm, e.g. a blanket over the shoulders (p.33)
Categorize as RTC (respiratory distress with accessory muscle use, p.7) and act with urgency
Packaged seated with oxygen / CPAP running and ready to load within 15 minutes; secondary survey en route
Delegate crew and wife effectively (doors, equipment, medication bag, stair chair)
triggers: partner, bring the cot to the bottom of the stairs

expected.actionEn: Move him seated by stair chair / carry device - he does not walk or exert himself (avoid exertion during transfers, p.33)
triggers: carry him down in the stair chair

expected.actionEn: Establish chief complaint: cannot catch his breath, woke up unable to breathe
HxC/C with OPQRST: sudden onset at night, trigger and relief (lying flat, sitting up), sputum, chest pain, fever, nausea/vomiting, trauma, medication adherence
triggers: does lying flat make it worse

expected.actionEn: Ask about chest pain and any pain (pain scale): none
PMHx (CHF, previous MI with stent, hypertension, high cholesterol)
Medications incl furosemide supply (ran out) and the nitroglycerin spray (not used tonight)

did he run out of any pills

expected.actionEn: Allergies (penicillin)
LOI

expected.actionEn: Use the wife as a second history source while he can only manage short phrases

BP by auscultation - high (172/98), so the SBP < 90 CPAP contraindication is absent

Initiate the CHF / Pulmonary Edema protocol with correct indications (CHF history + signs of pulmonary edema) and the baseline vitals already done: at rest, sitting upright with legs down, kept warm, oxygen to SpO2 94% or higher

Verbalize why nitroglycerin and ASA are not given: no chest pain, neither is among the p.33 interventions, the cardiac chest pain protocol (p.47) does not apply, and the p.73 / p.60 indications are absent
triggers: no nitroglycerin because no chest pain
cardiac chest pain protocol does not apply

expected.actionEn: Verbalize that no bronchodilator is among the p.33 interventions (no asthma/COPD history, so the p.49 protocol and ipratropium p.70 do not apply either) and that no fluid bolus is given: SBP 172 is far above the 90 the Hypovolemia protocol needs (p.54)
EMR: SpO2 stays below 94% on high-flow oxygen - assist ventilations with a BVM and oxygen (p.33, p.11)
triggers: SpO2 still below 94 so I'm bagging

expected.actionEn: PCP: state that every CPAP indication is met (age 13 or over, significant respiratory distress, awake and following commands, patent airway, RR 32 above 24, SpO2 89% below 94% on O2, accessory muscle use)

PCP: verbalize each CPAP contraindication as absent (age 12 or under; decreased LOC / cannot follow commands; respiratory arrest or hypoventilation; imminent respiratory failure; mask will not fit; vomiting or aspiration risk; traumatic cause; tracheostomy; pneumothorax; SBP below 90)

PCP: apply CPAP correctly - explain the mask, start at 5 L/min with the valve at 5 cmH2O, obtain a facial seal, reassess patient and vitals, then 2.5 cmH2O steps (7.5 cmH2O = 7 L/min) to a maximum of 10 cmH2O (8 L/min) (p.52-53)
Coach and reassure him: explain what each step is for and keep him calm and at rest
triggers: I'm going to put a mask on

expected.actionEn: Reassess ABCs and the effect of oxygen / CPAP after each CPAP adjustment
Reassess ABCs and mask seal / SpO2 after each major move (seated carry down the stairs, loading) (p.10)
Second full vitals within 5-6 minutes; interpret the improving trend
PCP: if he becomes drowsy, breathes slowly and shallowly, or SBP falls below 90, remove CPAP and ventilate with the BVM (PEEP valve 5 cmH2O to start) (p.52)
EMR: keep assisting ventilations while SpO2 is below 94%, stay upright and keep moving to hospital
En-route notification for a critical patient: acute pulmonary edema, respiratory distress, oxygen / CPAP, ETA
Complete hand-off: CHF history, ran out of furosemide, no chest pain, presentation, baseline versus repeat vitals
Treatments with times and response: oxygen, CPAP start time and settings (PCP) or assisted ventilations (EMR); no nitroglycerin, salbutamol or fluids given
Accurate PCR within 5 minutes (CPAP settings and times, SpO2 trend)

specialEvents.descriptionEn: BAD ACT: the candidate lays him back or flat/supine, reclines the stretcher or stair chair back, or tells him to lie down (the protocol requires sitting upright with the legs hung down). Keeping him upright, or tilting a chair only to move him while he stays seated, is NOT this event.
BAD ACT: the candidate lets or asks him to stand, walk or exert himself (to the stairs, down the stairs or out to the ambulance) instead of a seated carry with the equipment brought to him

PCP verbalizes checking the CPAP indications and contraindications before applying it (awake and following commands, systolic above 90, no vomiting or aspiration risk, no pneumothorax, no trauma, no tracheostomy, the mask fits)
PCP applies CPAP incorrectly: starts above 5 cmH2O, increases by more than 2.5 cmH2O per step, goes above the 10 cmH2O maximum, or leaves a poor facial seal uncorrected

AFTER the examiner has said that he has become drowsy with slow, shallow breathing, the PCP keeps the CPAP running or increases the pressure instead of removing it and ventilating with the BVM (PEEP valve 5 cmH2O to start)
PCP sets the PEEP valve above 5 cmH2O to start, increases it by more than 2.5 cmH2O per step, goes above 10 cmH2O, or keeps the PEEP valve on when the systolic falls below 90

drugs.doseEn: PCP only (p.33, p.51-53): start at 5 L/min with the CPAP valve at 5 cmH2O; obtain a facial seal; reassess patient and vitals; repeat in 2.5 cmH2O increments (7.5 cmH2O = 7 L/min, 10 cmH2O = 8 L/min) to a maximum of 10 cmH2O. If he deteriorates: remove CPAP and ventilate with a BVM (PEEP valve 5 cmH2O to start).
drugs.indicationsEn: 13 years or older in significant respiratory distress, awake and following commands, patent airway, and ALL of: RR above 24, SpO2 below 94% on oxygen, accessory muscle use - he qualifies
drugs.contraindicationsEn: 12 years or less; decreased LOC or inability to follow commands; respiratory arrest or hypoventilation / imminent respiratory failure; unable to fit the mask; vomiting or other aspiration risk; traumatic cause; tracheostomy; suspected or known pneumothorax; systolic BP below 90 - none apply

drugs.doseEn: NOT INDICATED in this scenario: the monograph indication is chest discomfort that appears cardiac in nature (p.73) and he has no chest pain; nitroglycerin is not among the p.33 interventions. His own spray is in the medication bag. If it is actually given, record drug:nitroglycerin.
NOT INDICATED in this scenario: the indication is chest pain or atypical symptoms of cardiac ischemia (p.60) and there are none. If it is actually given, record drug:asa.

NOT INDICATED in this scenario: p.33 lists no bronchodilator for CHF / pulmonary edema and he has no asthma/COPD history; the wheeze sits among bilateral crackles from pulmonary edema. If it is actually given, record drug:salbutamol.
NOT INDICATED in this scenario: the indication is severe bronchospasm in asthma and COPD (p.70) and he has neither. If it is actually given, record drug:ipratropium.
NOT INDICATED in this scenario: the Hypovolemia protocol needs a systolic BP below 90 and signs of shock (p.54); his is 172. If a bolus is actually given, record drug:fluid-bolus.

trackNotes.emrEn: EMR: sit him upright with the legs hung down, keep him at rest and warm, high-flow oxygen by NRB (add a nasal cannula under the mask if SpO2 stays below 94%), assist ventilations with a BVM if SpO2 is still below 94% (p.33), and RTC with a seated carry. No CPAP or PEEP valve (PCP only). The patient's own nitroglycerin spray is not given: the CHF protocol (p.33) does not list it and the p.73 indication (chest discomfort that appears cardiac) is absent. (Textbook practice - not a BC rubric item: some systems use nitroglycerin for hypertensive pulmonary edema; the BC guideline does not.) Salbutamol is not given for the wheeze (p.33 lists no bronchodilator; textbook practice - not a BC rubric item: wheeze among bilateral crackles from pulmonary edema is not bronchospasm). No Functional Enquiry. EMR set 2 (alternate values, after assisted ventilations by BVM and no CPAP): respirations 28, still laboured, SpO2 92% - keep assisting ventilations and transport; the engine speaks the PCP values on CPAP.
trackNotes.pcpEn: PCP adds, on scene, CPAP (state every indication, rule out every contraindication aloud; start 5 cmH2O at 5 L/min, facial seal, reassess, 2.5 cmH2O steps to a maximum of 10 cmH2O at 8 L/min), the BVM with a PEEP valve (5 cmH2O to start) if he deteriorates, and the 9-system Functional Enquiry en route. The CHF protocol does not call for vascular access, and a fluid bolus is NOT indicated (SBP 172, not below 90).

sourcePages: scenario md-10 (data/practical/scenarios-2.json); BC Provincial Examination Guidelines (current to June 15, 2026): p.6 Patient Assessment Model (load and transport may be appropriate any time after the decision point), p.7 Findings in Unstable Adult Patients (respiratory distress / accessory muscle use), p.10 load and transport (reassess ABCI after each major move; consider additional resources such as first responders), p.11 Primary survey interventions (assisting inadequate or failing respirations; oxygen), p.33 Congestive Heart Failure or Pulmonary Edema (keep at rest and avoid exertion during transfers, bring equipment to the patient, sit upright with legs hung down, keep warm, oxygen to SpO2 94% or above, assist ventilations if SpO2 below 94%, transport; PCP: consider CPAP on scene, BVM with PEEP valve 5 cmH2O to start), p.47 Cardiac Chest Pain, p.49 SOB with a history of asthma/COPD, p.50 Oxygen (non-rebreather 15 L/min plus nasal cannula), p.51-53 CPAP (indications, contraindications, use, setting table, PEEP use), p.54 Hypovolemia (SBP below 90), p.60 Aspirin, p.70 Ipratropium, p.73 Nitroglycerin, p.77 Salbutamol; EMALB grading criteria timing rules (priority: ready to load within 15 minutes; vitals interval 7-8 / over 9 minutes)
